q: In the figure, which foundation is a strap (cantilever) footing?
o: Footing D
Footing B
Footing C
Footing E
n: D has two separate pads joined by a stiff strap beam. The exterior column sits at the property line, off-center on its pad; the strap ties it to the interior footing so the eccentric load does not tip the pad.

q: What is a combined footing?
o: A footing that supports one column only
A single footing that supports two or more columns
A footing made of both concrete and steel
A footing placed on piles
n: A combined footing carries two or more columns on one slab, usually rectangular or trapezoidal in plan. It is used when separate footings would overlap or one column is at the property line.

q: In the figure, which foundation is an isolated (spread) footing?
o: Footing B
Footing D
Footing A
Footing E
n: A is a single pad under one column, the most common and cheapest footing where the soil is reasonably good and columns are well apart.

q: As a concrete column becomes more slender, how does its mode of failure change?
o: From buckling toward crushing
It does not change
From shear failure toward torsion failure
From crushing of the material toward buckling (instability)
n: A short, stocky column fails when its concrete crushes and steel yields. A slender column bends sideways under load (second-order effects), which adds moment and lowers its strength, and at the extreme it buckles.

q: Why are drop panels or column capitals added to a flat slab?
o: To thicken the slab at the column and raise its punching-shear strength
To make the ceiling look higher
To reduce the self-weight of the slab
To replace the column ties
n: Around a column, the slab carries a concentrated reaction that can punch through it. A drop panel (a thicker area) or a flared capital enlarges the critical section and raises the shear capacity. Drop panels also help with negative moment.

q: A slab panel supported on all four edges measures 3 m × 7 m. How does it behave?
o: As a two-way slab, since it is supported on four sides
As a one-way slab, since the long-to-short span ratio is 2 or more
As a flat slab
As a cantilever slab
n: The ratio is 7/3 = 2.33. When the long span is at least twice the short span, the short direction is so much stiffer that nearly all the load goes that way, so the panel is designed as one-way.
steps: Long span L = 7 m, short span S = 3 m

q: In the figure, which foundation is a mat (raft)?
o: Footing B
Footing C
Footing E
Footing A
n: E is one thick slab under all the columns. Mats spread the building load over the whole footprint.

q: When is a combined footing a good choice?
o: When the columns are very far apart on strong rock
When there is only one column
When the building has no columns
When separate footings would overlap, or a column sits at the property line
n: If two footings would overlap, or an exterior column cannot have a footing projecting past the property line, joining them in one footing gives a centred resultant and even soil pressure.

q: What is a pad footing?
o: A simple isolated footing of uniform thickness under one column
A footing under a whole wall
A footing that supports all the columns
A pile cap on four piles
n: A pad footing is the simplest isolated footing: a flat block of concrete of one thickness. Stepped and sloped footings are variations that save concrete.

q: Under NSCP 2015, when may slenderness effects be neglected in a column not braced against sidesway?
o: When kLu/r ≤ 100
When kLu/r ≤ 22
When the column is shorter than 3 m
Never
n: For sway columns, slenderness may be ignored when kLu/r ≤ 22. For braced columns the limit is 34 + 12(M1/M2), but no more than 40. Above these limits, moments must be magnified for second-order effects.

q: What is punching shear?
o: A bending failure at midspan
The failure of a beam's stirrups
A two-way shear failure where a column pushes through a slab or footing
The crushing of the column concrete
n: Punching shear forms a truncated cone or pyramid around the column. It governs the thickness of flat slabs and footings and is checked at d/2 from the column face.

q: What is a two-way slab?
o: A slab with two layers of bars
A slab supported on two sides only
A slab with two different thicknesses
A slab that carries its load in two perpendicular directions to its supports
n: When a panel is supported on four sides and nearly square (long/short span below 2), it bends in both directions, so bars are placed both ways.

q: When is a mat (raft) foundation most suitable?
o: When the soil is weak, column loads are heavy, or settlement must be kept even
When the soil is solid rock and loads are light
When there is only one column
When the building is a single-storey shed
n: If separate footings would cover more than about half the footprint, a single mat is simpler. It spreads the load, lowers bearing pressure and bridges soft spots to limit differential settlement.

q: In the figure, which foundation is a rectangular combined footing?
o: Footing C
Footing B
Footing D
Footing A
n: B carries two columns on one rectangular slab. It works when the column loads are similar or when the footing can extend past both columns so the resultant falls at its center.

q: What is a stepped footing?
o: A footing placed on a staircase
A footing under a stair
An isolated footing whose thickness decreases in steps away from the column
Two footings at different levels joined by a beam
n: A stepped footing is thick near the column, where moment and shear are highest, and thinner at the edges. The steps save concrete while keeping enough depth where it is needed.

q: What is the radius of gyration r of a rectangular column section of depth h, used in the slenderness ratio kLu/r?
o: About 0.5h
About 0.1h
Equal to h
About 0.3h
n: For a rectangle, r = h/√12 ≈ 0.289h, which NSCP lets you round to 0.30h in the direction being checked. For a circular column r = 0.25 times the diameter.

q: What is a waffle slab?
o: A two-way slab with a grid of closely spaced ribs running both ways
A slab with ribs in one direction only
A flat slab with drop panels
A slab on grade
n: Waffle (two-way joist) slabs are cast over dome forms, leaving a grid of ribs under a thin top slab. They span far with little weight and are often left exposed as a ceiling.

q: A slab panel supported on all four edges measures 5 m × 6 m. How does it behave?
o: As a one-way slab
As a two-way slab, since the long-to-short span ratio is less than 2
As a cantilever slab
As a flat slab without supports
n: The ratio is 6/5 = 1.2, less than 2, so both directions carry a large share of the load, and bars are designed both ways.
steps: Long span L = 6 m, short span S = 5 m

q: What is a one-way slab?
o: A slab with bars in both directions of equal size
A slab supported directly on columns
A slab that bends and carries its load mainly in one direction
A slab with no reinforcement
n: A one-way slab spans like a wide beam between two supports. Its main bars run in the span direction, and only temperature and shrinkage bars run the other way.

q: In the figure, which foundation is a trapezoidal combined footing?
o: Footing B
Footing D
Footing E
Footing C
n: C is wider under the heavier column at the property line. The trapezoid moves the footing's centroid toward the heavier load, so the resultant stays centred and the soil pressure stays uniform even though the footing cannot extend past the property line.

q: What is a sloped footing?
o: An isolated footing whose top surface slopes down from the column toward its edges
A footing built on a hillside
A footing tilted to face the wind
A footing under a ramp
n: A sloped footing tapers from full depth at the column to a thinner edge, saving concrete like a stepped footing. It is harder to form and cast because the slope must hold its shape.

q: Which way of bracing a column raises its buckling capacity the most?
o: Leaving both ends pinned and free to sway
Restraining its ends against rotation and sway (fixed and braced)
Making the column taller
Using a larger bar spacing
n: The buckling load is π²EI/(kL)². Fixing the ends and preventing sway lowers the effective length factor k (toward 0.5), which can raise the capacity up to four times compared with pinned ends.

q: What is a one-way ribbed (joist) slab?
o: A slab with ribs in two directions
A slab carried directly by columns
A thin slab on closely spaced parallel ribs that span in one direction
A slab that rests on soil
n: Joist construction removes concrete from the tension zone, leaving ribs under a thin slab. It is lighter than a solid slab of the same depth and suits longer one-way spans.

q: What is a flat slab?
o: A slab on grade
A slab carried by beams on all four sides
A slab with ribs both ways
A slab carried directly by columns without beams, usually with drop panels or capitals
n: Flat slabs rest straight on columns, giving flat ceilings and lower floor-to-floor heights. Drop panels or capitals handle the high shear and moment at the columns. A flat plate is the same system without them.

q: How is a one-way slab usually supported?
o: Mainly on two opposite sides
Directly on columns only
On all four sides with equal spans
On a single central support
n: A slab supported on two opposite edges (or on four edges with a long-to-short span ratio of 2 or more) spans one way. Load goes straight across to the two supports.
